title: Binary Search Trees
relevance: BSTs underpin ordered dynamic sets/maps and a large class of OA/interview tree problems that exploit the inorder-sorted property and O(h) path-based operations.

phases.goal: Establish the BST ordering invariant, the inorder-sorted property, and the height-based cost model.

must_hit.point: For every node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys in the right subtree are strictly larger than the node's key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the left-<node and right->node rule for every node, not only immediate children.

must_hit.point: An inorder traversal of a BST yields keys in sorted order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out inorder as producing a sorted stream and notes many BST problems reduce to that.

must_hit.point: Search, insert, and delete take O(h) time; if the tree is balanced then h = log n so operations are O(log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties runtime to height h and states balanced height gives logarithmic operations.

must_hit.point: A standard BST is not guaranteed balanced; inserting in sorted or reverse-sorted order can skew it into a linked list with O(n) operations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the degeneration trap and the O(n) cost on a skewed tree.

probes: What property must hold at every node for a binary tree to be a BST, and what does that imply for inorder traversal and operation cost?

hints.1: Start from the left/right key ordering around a single node.
hints.2: Connect that ordering to inorder output and to path length from root.
hints.3: State left < node < right globally, inorder is sorted, ops are O(h), and unbalanced insert order can make h = n.

phases.goal: Show how BST ordering drives search, extrema, floor/ceil, insert, delete, validation, LCA, and order-statistic walks.

must_hit.point: Search compares the target to the current node and discards an entire subtree at each step, running in O(h) time and O(1) auxiliary space iteratively.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes go-left if smaller / go-right if larger until match or null.

must_hit.point: The minimum is the leftmost node and the maximum is the rightmost node, each found in O(h) time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Follow left children for min and right children for max.

must_hit.point: Ceil is the smallest value ≥ key and floor is the largest value ≤ key; both walk one path updating a candidate when branching toward a tighter valid bound.
must_hit.evidence_hint: On a greater node for ceil, record candidate and go left; on a lesser node for floor, record candidate and go right.

must_hit.point: Insert walks to the nullptr leaf position implied by comparisons and attaches the new node as left or right child.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains finding the empty child slot without rebuilding the tree.

must_hit.point: Delete has three cases: leaf remove; one child replace with that child; two children replace with inorder successor (min of right subtree) or predecessor then delete that node.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all three cases and names successor/predecessor for the two-child case.

must_hit.point: Validating a BST requires every node to lie in a strict (min, max) range updated from ancestors, not only local parent–child comparisons.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions passing tightened bounds left/right and rejecting local-only checks.

must_hit.point: LCA in a BST is the first node whose value lies between p and q inclusive; both smaller go left, both larger go right, else current is LCA.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks from the root using ordering until the split point.

must_hit.point: Kth smallest follows inorder and stops at the k-th visit; kth largest uses reverse inorder (right, root, left), in O(h + k) time bounded by O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties kth order statistics to (reverse) inorder early stop.

probes: Walk through how you search, find floor/ceil, insert, and delete in a BST—especially the two-children delete case—and how you validate the tree.
How do you find the LCA of two nodes and the kth smallest value using BST structure?

hints.1: Use comparisons to choose one child and discard the other subtree.
hints.2: Separate leaf / one-child / two-child delete, and contrast local vs range validation.
hints.3: Two-child delete copies successor then deletes it; validate with (min,max); LCA is the split node; kth uses inorder counting.

phases.goal: Contrast BSTs with hash sets and space/time choices when exploiting ordered traversal.

must_hit.point: A hash set gives O(1) average insert/lookup but no ordering; a BST supports floor, ceiling, successor, and range-style ordered queries.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly trades constant-time unordered ops for ordered BST operations.

must_hit.point: C++ std::set and std::map are balanced BSTs (Red-Black Trees), so they keep the dynamic ordered-set cost model in practice.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names std::set/map as balanced BST implementations.

must_hit.point: A BST iterator can precompute full inorder in O(n) space for O(1) next, or simulate inorder with a stack bounded by O(h) and O(1) amortized next.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares eager array materialization versus height-bounded stack simulation.

probes: When would you choose a BST over a hash set, and how would you trade space versus next()-cost for an inorder iterator?

hints.1: Think about whether you need order, not only membership.
hints.2: Compare unordered O(1) average ops with floor/ceil/successor support.
hints.3: Hash set: fast, unordered; BST: ordered queries; iterator: O(n) preload vs O(h) stack with amortized O(1) next.

phases.goal: Apply BST properties to construction, streaming inorder, two-sum, successor, and recovering swapped nodes.

must_hit.point: Constructing a BST from preorder can run in O(n) by consuming the array once with a dynamic upper bound instead of repeated inserts in O(n^2).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes bound-guided linear build versus insert-each-element rebuild.

must_hit.point: Inorder successor/predecessor can be found in O(h) by walking from the root and tracking the best greater/lesser candidate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: On successor, when current > key record and go left; otherwise go right (predecessor symmetric).

must_hit.point: Two-sum in a BST can mimic two pointers with forward and reverse inorder iterators, using O(h) space instead of materializing an O(n) sorted array.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions dual iterators and advancing the end whose sum is too small or too large.

must_hit.point: With exactly two nodes swapped, inorder finds one or two violations via a prev pointer; swap first with last if distant, or first with middle if adjacent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains first/middle/last anomaly marking during inorder and the final value swap.

probes: How do you build a BST from preorder in linear time, find successors, solve two-sum without an array, and recover a tree with two swapped nodes?

hints.1: Lean on inorder as a sorted stream and on bounds while scanning preorder.
hints.2: For two-sum, think two pointers on that stream; for recover, look for dips vs prev.
hints.3: Preorder+upper bound O(n); successor walk O(h); dual iterators O(h); recover marks first/middle/last then swaps.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Hash sets give O(1) average insert/lookup but no order; BSTs keep ordered ops (floor, ceiling, successor, ranges). In C++, std::set/std::map are balanced BSTs (Red-Black) providing dynamic ordered-set behavior.

tradeoffs.topic: Eager inorder array vs height-bounded BST iterator
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Precomputing full inorder uses O(n) space for O(1) next(); a stack that pushes left spines uses O(h) space with O(1) amortized next() because each node is pushed and popped once.

tradeoffs.topic: Repeated insert vs bound-guided preorder construction
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Inserting each preorder value sequentially can cost O(n^2); walking the array once with a dynamic upper bound builds the tree in O(n).

gotchas.trap: Assuming a standard BST is always O(log n) because binary search is logarithmic.
gotchas.correction: Cost is O(h). Sorted or reverse-sorted inserts can skew the tree into a linked list with O(n) search/insert/delete.

gotchas.trap: Validating a BST by only checking each node against its immediate children.
gotchas.correction: A deep right-subtree node can violate the global root bound; enforce a strict (min, max) range at every node, tightening max on left and min on right.

gotchas.trap: Deleting a two-child node by only unlinking it or swapping with an arbitrary neighbor.
gotchas.correction: Replace its value with the inorder successor (minimum of the right subtree) or predecessor, then delete that successor/predecessor node.

gotchas.trap: Treating recover-BST as sorting the whole tree structure or only fixing one adjacent dip.
gotchas.correction: Exactly two values are swapped; inorder yields one or two violations—swap first with last if two dips, or first with middle if the swapped pair was adjacent.
